title: Episode 196: George W. Bush: The Florida Recount, September 11, and Ground Zero (2000–2001)
description:
George W. Bush entered the presidency through the most dramatic, nerve-shredding election crisis in modern history: the thirty-six-day Florida recount of 2000, decided by just five hundred and thirty-seven votes and an epic Supreme Court battle over 'hanging chads.' Yet eight months into his presidency, on a brilliant blue Tuesday morning, September 11, 2001, the world changed forever. While reading to second-graders in Sarasota, Florida, Chief of Staff Andy Card whispered into Bush's ear: 'A second plane hit the second tower. America is under attack.' Three days later, standing atop a crushed fire engine amidst the smoldering ruins of the World Trade Center with a megaphone in hand, Bush rallied a grieving nation with an unscripted, immortal shout: 'I can hear you! The rest of the world hears you! And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon!' Discover the crucible that transformed George W. Bush.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the crucible of the twenty-first century with George W. Bush. From the razor-thin drama of the 2000 Florida recount to the catastrophic tragedy of September 11, Bush faced crises that reshaped American history and global security. Here is George with the story of the hanging chads, the Sarasota classroom, and the bullhorn at Ground Zero.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE TEXAS GOVERNOR AND COMPASSIONATE CONSERVATISM
George Walker Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, in July 1946, the eldest son of George H.W. and Barbara Bush. Raised in the wide-open plains of Midland and Houston, Texas, young '43' inherited his father's athletic charm and his mother's sharp, blunt wit. Graduating from Yale and earning an MBA from Harvard Business School, Bush spent his twenties and thirties working in the independent Texas oil business, known as a charismatic, gregarious carouser who loved Mexican food and country music. In 1986, at age forty, profoundly influenced by a spiritual conversation with evangelist Billy Graham and the loving devotion of his wife Laura, Bush quit drinking cold turkey and dedicated his life to evangelical Christian faith and disciplined public purpose. Purchasing a stake in the Texas Rangers baseball team, Bush became a beloved public figure, sitting in the front rows of the ballpark in Arlington eating hot dogs and chatting with fans. In 1994, he stunned political experts by defeating popular Democratic Governor Ann Richards, governing Texas for six successful years with bipartisan warmth under the philosophy of 'compassionate conservatism.' His transformation in Midland from an aimless young oilman into a disciplined, sober leader of faith set the moral foundation for his future political career. The journey from Texas oilman to governor showed an intuitive leader who understood the hopes and values of everyday working families. His early career taught him that authentic character, loyalty, and faith are the true compass points that guide a leader through political adversity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE 36-DAY FLORIDA RECOUNT: NOVEMBER 2000
On election night, November 7, 2000, the presidential race between Governor George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore produced the most astonishing, chaotic deadlock in American history. Television networks initially projected Florida for Gore, retracted it, called Florida for Bush, and then retracted it again as the margin shrank to microscopic proportions. By morning, out of nearly six million ballots cast in Florida, Bush led by a mere seventeen hundred votes. For thirty-six agonizing days, the presidency hung upon manual recounts in Palm Beach, Broward, and Miami-Dade counties. The American public was introduced to an entire lexicon of election mechanics: 'hanging chads,' 'dimpled chads,' and confusing 'butterfly ballots.' Legal armies led by James A. Baker III for Bush and David Boies for Gore fought dozens of court battles. Finally, on December 12, 2000, in the landmark ruling Bush versus Gore, the Supreme Court voted five to four to halt the statewide manual recounts. Bush carried Florida by precisely five hundred and thirty-seven votes, winning the electoral college two hundred and seventy-one to two hundred and sixty-six, despite Gore winning the popular vote. The extraordinary drama of the Florida recount demonstrated the remarkable stability of American constitutional institutions, peacefully resolving a disputed election without civil unrest. The Florida recount showed the remarkable restraint and civic patience of the American electorate, accepting judicial resolution without violence. The resolution of the 2000 election proved that the American rule of law is stronger than any political ambition or electoral dispute.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SARASOTA CLASSROOM: SEPTEMBER 11, 2001
On the morning of Tuesday, September 11, 2001, President Bush was visiting Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida, to promote his signature education initiative. While waiting to enter the second-grade classroom, senior advisor Karl Rove informed him that a twin-engine commercial airliner had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York. Assuming it was an awful weather accident or navigational error, Bush sat in a small wooden chair in front of sixteen children to listen to their reading lesson from 'The Pet Goat.' At nine-o-five in the morning, White House Chief of Staff Andy Card entered the room, walked silently across the carpet, and leaned down to whisper into Bush's right ear seven words that shattered the modern world: 'A second plane hit the second tower. America is under attack.' Bush remained seated for seven deliberate minutes, maintaining complete outward calm so as not to terrify the children or alert the waiting press corps, his jaw clenched and eyes grave, knowing that his presidency had irrevocably changed. That quiet moment of composure in the Sarasota classroom revealed a Commander-in-Chief who understood the importance of projecting calm during an unfolding national catastrophe. In the silence of that classroom, Bush shouldered the immense weight of supreme command, preparing to lead the free world through an unprecedented war. That quiet moment in the classroom showed a leader possessing the iron self-control necessary to guide a nation through unprecedented peril.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: FLIGHT OF THE INTRUDERS: SEPTEMBER 11'S ODYSSEY
Rushing to a secure holding room in the school, Bush addressed the nation in a brief, solemn broadcast before being whisked away by the Secret Service to Sarasota Airport. Taking off aboard Air Force One at ten-thirty-five, the presidential aircraft climbed to forty-five thousand feet and began an erratic, day-long odyssey across the country amid terrifying, unverified intelligence reports that the White House, the Capitol, and Air Force One itself were designated targets. The Pentagon had been struck by a third hijacked airliner, and United Flight 93 had crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after heroic passengers fought back. To protect the continuity of government, Secret Service agents refused to let Bush return to Washington, flying instead to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Furious and demanding to return home, Bush firmly overruled his security team: 'I'm coming back to Washington. I don't want whoever did this thinking they've chased the President out of town.' At seven o'clock that evening, Marine One touched down on the South Lawn against the smoking silhouette of the Pentagon. Bush's firm refusal to remain in hiding on September 11 demonstrated his unyielding determination to project presidential strength and continuity in the nation's capital. Returning to Washington that evening, Bush demonstrated that the seat of American government would never yield to terrorist intimidation. His return to the capital affirmed that the American republic would never be bowed, cowed, or deterred by acts of cowardice and terror.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BULLHORN AT GROUND ZERO: SEPTEMBER 14, 2001
On Friday, September 14, three days after the attacks, President Bush flew by helicopter to lower Manhattan to visit the smoldering, sixteen-acre graveyard of twisted steel and pulverized concrete known as 'Ground Zero.' Walking through the ash amidst exhausted rescue workers, firefighters, and ironworkers, Bush climbed onto the crushed, soot-blackened chassis of Fire Truck 16. A retired firefighter named Bob Beckwith, standing on the wreckage, handed the President a bullhorn and draped an arm around his waist. As Bush began to speak, rescue workers in the back of the crowd cupped their ears and shouted: 'We can't hear you!' Bush looked toward the voice, lowered the bullhorn for an instant, then raised it to his lips and roared with unscripted, electric fury: 'I can hear you! The rest of the world hears you! And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon!' The crowd erupted into thunderous, weeping cheers, pounding steel beams and chanting: 'U-S-A! U-S-A!' In that singular, raw human moment, Bush united the nation in grief and resolve. Standing atop that crushed fire engine at Ground Zero, George W. Bush captured the grief and righteous anger of an entire nation with an unscripted, immortal shout. That moment on the pile at Ground Zero became one of the defining images of American history, symbolizing the unbreakable resilience of the nation. The spontaneous cry through the megaphone at Ground Zero became the rallying cry of a free people rising up to defend their civilization.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE ADDRESS TO CONGRESS: SEPTEMBER 20, 2001
Six days later, on September 20, 2001, President Bush walked into the chamber of the House of Representatives to deliver the most consequential address of his life. Facing a joint session of Congress and ninety million television viewers, Bush looked into the cameras and framed the global War on Terror: 'Our war on terror begins with al-Qaeda, but it does not end there. It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.' He paid moving tribute to Todd Beamer, the heroic passenger aboard United 93 whose final recorded words were 'Let's roll,' holding up the police shield of Officer George Howard, who had perished in the towers, given to him by the officer's mother. In that hour, partisan politics completely vanished; leaders of both parties hugged on the floor, and Bush's public approval rating soared to ninety percent—the highest in Gallup polling history. That address to the joint session of Congress rallied a united nation behind the defense of freedom, defining the struggle against global terrorism for a generation. The address before Congress articulated a clear moral doctrine: that nations of the world must choose between freedom and the forces of terror. That joint session address was a masterpiece of moral clarity, uniting Democrats and Republicans in a shared defense of constitutional liberty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TRANSFORMATIVE CRUCIBLE OF 43
In the span of ten harrowing days in September 2001, George W. Bush was transformed from a disputed, accidental president into a wartime Commander-in-Chief. He authorized the deployment of Special Operations forces and CIA operatives to Afghanistan to topple the Taliban regime, created the Department of Homeland Security, and signed the USA PATRIOT Act. The jovial Texas rancher who had dreamed of educational reform was now tasked with defending a wounded superpower against an elusive, stateless enemy. His resolve was total, guided by a deep personal conviction that freedom is not America's gift to the world, but the Almighty God's gift to each man and woman in this world. The crucible of Ground Zero had forged an indelible bond between George W. Bush and the American people that would define the turbulent decade to come. In the crucible of September 11, George W. Bush was forged into a wartime president whose leadership would shape the geopolitical trajectory of the modern world. In the darkest days of modern American history, George W. Bush provided the moral resolve and steady hand that held a traumatized country together. The crucible of September 11 defined George W. Bush's historical destiny, placing him at the helm of an epic global crusade for human freedom.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
George W. Bush rallied a traumatized superpower from the smoking rubble of Ground Zero, uniting a grief-stricken nation behind his leadership. But the road ahead brought complex wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, historic humanitarian breakthroughs in Africa, and unforgettable cultural moments. Next week, we continue our George W. Bush saga: the historic first pitch at Yankee Stadium, the creation of PEPFAR saving twenty-five million lives in Africa, and his famous mountain bike rides on his Crawford ranch. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
